I've farmed this land in Quzhou my whole life. My father grew wheat and maize, and so did his father. I know this soil and I know this climate. The winters are dry and cold, the summers are hot. The water table has been dropping for years — I've noticed I have to pump longer than I used to. But this is what I know how to do.

I have about 8 mu of contracted land. The rotation here is always the same: winter wheat, then summer maize. Everyone does it. The grain station buys it, the input dealers sell me seed and fertilizer for it, and I know the calendar by heart — wheat goes in around October, comes out in June, then I rush to get maize in the ground right after.

For wheat, I'll use an improved variety. The pure traditional stuff doesn't yield well enough anymore and the seeds are hard to get anyway. For maize, I always buy hybrid — Zhengdan 958 or whatever the dealer has. Hybrids give better ears.

I put down plenty of fertilizer. I know the extension workers say I use too much nitrogen, but I've seen what happens when the wheat turns yellow from lack of feed — I'd rather waste a little than lose the crop. I apply urea as a base before planting wheat, then topdress at jointing. For maize I throw fertilizer in at planting and again when it's knee-high.

I irrigate wheat three times — once before sowing to wet the seedbed, once at jointing in spring, once at heading. Maize usually gets by on summer rain but I'll irrigate once if August is dry.

I spray herbicide on both crops and hit the wheat with a fungicide if I see rust spots spreading in the village. Maize I'll spray for aphids if they get bad.

For tillage, I hire the rotary tiller after maize harvest to prepare the wheat field. After wheat harvest I go straight to maize with no tillage — there's no time.
